title: Mississippi Delta — a slick that isn't

gallery.blurb: 47 km² of dark water, 9 dB below the sea around it, twenty times longer than it is wide. Is it oil?

notes: Zenodo Part III look-alike scene (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.13761290, CC-BY — the attribution is mandatory and must appear on a slide). This case exists to be REJECTED, and it pays for the whole detection stage: by every geometric feature the detector measures it looks like a spill — 47 km², -9.05 dB contrast, elongation 21.2 — and it is not one. LOCATION IS REAL: the tile carries EPSG:4326 and a real geotransform, so bounds.json holds its true box (W -89.6488 S 29.1688 E -89.4649 N 29.3527). That location is itself the explanation — the Mississippi Delta is full of natural seeps and rigs, which is exactly why this is a convincing look-alike rather than an arbitrary dark patch. TIME IS NOT KNOWN: the TIFF carries no acquisition timestamp (the only tag is AREA_OR_POINT), so detection_time is a deliberate 1970 epoch sentinel. provenance is 'benchmark', so the CNN scene classifier scored this scene and its confidence is a model probability, not a rule margin (Master §6.3). Rejected at P(oil) 0.0020, threshold 0.143. Expected Stage 1 output: a FeatureCollection with zero features classified 'oil' — the dark region may legitimately appear as a 'lookalike' feature. Bundle built by Soumirya and PASSES the validator (13 Sept); held out of cases/index.json pending the presentation-order decision. RADAR CONTACTS: the ship detector finds 1 contact after land masking, at [-89.54732, 29.35262] (26 px, -5.93 dB). It is a genuine return — 29.7σ above the sea — sitting in the raster's top pixel row near the Delta shoreline; what it is (structure or vessel) has not been established. It is an UNATTRIBUTED radar contact and must never be called a dark vessel: darkness needs an AIS cross-check at a known time, and this scene has no acquisition time (Master §6.3, D34).
